questions.scenario: A Terraform plan shows `-/+ resource "aws_db_instance" ... (forces replacement)`.
questions.question: What does that mean?
options: The database will be patched in place
Only its tags change
Terraform will delete the database and create a new one; stop and reconsider
Terraform will take a snapshot
questions.explanation: Read every plan; production databases get deletion protection and prevent_destroy.

questions.scenario: Two engineers run terraform apply at the same time against state stored on one laptop.
questions.question: What should the team have?
options: Remote state in S3 with versioning and locking (use_lockfile)
State committed to Git
Separate state per engineer
No state at all
questions.explanation: Remote, locked, versioned state prevents corruption and loss.

questions.scenario: CI needs to run terraform plan against AWS.
questions.question: What is the recommended way to authenticate?
options: An IAM user's access keys in GitHub secrets
The root account
GitHub's OIDC token to assume a scoped IAM role for the job
A password in the workflow file
questions.explanation: OIDC gives short-lived credentials with no stored keys.

questions.scenario: Argo CD has selfHeal on. An engineer scales fraud to 3 replicas with kubectl during an incident.
questions.question: What happens?
options: Argo CD deletes the namespace
The change stays until the next merge
Argo CD sends an email and does nothing
Argo CD puts fraud back to what Git says; the fix must be made as a pull request
questions.explanation: Self-heal keeps the cluster equal to Git, which makes every change reviewable.

questions.scenario: How does a new image version reach production in a GitOps setup?
questions.question: Which flow is correct?
options: CI runs helm upgrade against production directly
CI pushes the image, then a pull request changes the tag in the production values; merging it lets Argo CD roll it out
An engineer edits the Deployment with kubectl
Argo CD pulls the newest image automatically from any registry
questions.explanation: Deployments become commits with authors, reviews and reverts.

questions.scenario: Which file should be committed alongside the Terraform code?
questions.question: Choose one.
options: .terraform.lock.hcl, which pins provider versions
.terraform/ with downloaded providers
terraform.tfstate
backend.hcl with the state bucket's details for your account
questions.explanation: The lock file makes everyone and CI use the same provider versions; state, caches and local config stay out.

questions.scenario: A team uses Terraform both for the VPC and to deploy every application release.
questions.question: What's the problem?
options: Terraform can't create Kubernetes objects
It's too fast
Application changes many times a day share a pipeline and state with rarely changed, high-risk infrastructure; keep them separate
Argo CD forbids it
questions.explanation: Terraform for cloud resources, GitOps for platform add-ons and applications.

questions.scenario: Why might a bank choose OpenTofu over Terraform?
questions.question: Which reason is accurate?
options: It's the only tool supporting AWS
It's open source under MPL after Terraform's move to the Business Source Licence in 2023, and reads the same code
It doesn't need state
It's built into Kubernetes
questions.explanation: Licensing, not features, is the usual reason.
